paragraphs.text: A eulogy delivered by Saint Apa Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, in the martyr shrine built in the name of Saint Mercurius, on the day of his holy commemoration, the twentieth of the month of Hathor, in which he praised the many mighty deeds and wonders that took place through the holy martyr Saint Mercurius. In the peace of God. May his holy blessings be with us all together. Amen.

Truly, light has dawned for the righteous, for this Saint Mercurius, according to [?] The sacred psalmist and father of Christ according to the flesh, the righteous king and singer of hymns, David, said it,
crying out, crying out in his sweet voice, playing his lyre with the plectrum in his hand, saying, “Light has dawned for the righteous.”
And again, “Light has dawned in the darkness for the upright in heart.”
Christ himself said in the Gospel, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”
Saint Mercurius [?] you see [?] boundless [?] that you were a pagan before you knew Christ well.
And when he had armed himself, he was going out to war against the barbarians,
going ahead of Decius, the lawless king, as commander of the army,
holding the arrows of the bow with which he would shoot the barbarians.

But the angel of the Lord came down from heaven and gave him the sword, saying, “Destroy the barbarians.” [?] “It is fitting that we show great devotion toward them and give them honor and glory as they deserve, with libations and sacrifices, in return for the good things they did for us before.

We command that the doors of all the temples be opened, in every city and every village, from the Roman Empire southward to Philae and the Ethiopians, and that incense be offered to the honored gods and their worship be performed with great zeal,

so that no Christian may appear anywhere. The provincial governors are to pursue these Christians everywhere, whether bishops, priests, readers, monks, laypeople, men, women, soldiers, whether civilians or officials—in short, every kind of person—by the authority of my kingship, so that they sacrifice to the honored gods.
Whoever opposes my command is to be handed over to severe and varied tortures until they die.”

Then Decius, the lawless king, ordered the herald to cry out throughout the whole city, “Greetings to all you people! Whether soldiers or civilians, people of every kind and every age, come, all of you, [?] the temple of the gods, and offer sacrifices to them.” They lit the firewood at the entrance of the temple and offered sacrifices and incense to them, along with calves, rams, and birds. The sky was filled with the smoke of the stench of their sacrifices.
There was great turmoil among the Christians: they were being pursued, beaten, dragged to the gateways and the courts, and forced to sacrifice.

There were great disturbances everywhere, for the tyrant had ordered every kind of terrifying instrument of torture to be set before him. so that the Christians would see them and be afraid: sharpened swords and iron beds, and instruments for stretching sinews, and blades for cutting out tongues, and cleavers, and heated spikes, and bronze cauldrons full of boiling pitch, and also bronze cauldrons full of poison, and torture wheels, and all the other terrifying instruments of punishment.

For that impious emperor used to say, “Whoever opposes my command, I will gouge out his eyes, cut out his tongue, and extract his marrow. I will saw off his toes and remove his brain. As for the rest of his body, I will throw it into the fire for it to consume.”
When the devout people saw these things, great faintheartedness overcame them. They were afraid and gave up,

each one handing over his neighbor to death, and parents handing over their children to death. They forgot natural affection. Brothers dragged one another away, threw one another down, and handed one another over. There was great turmoil
for everyone who confessed the name, the name of Jesus.
Now there was a brave young man in the army named Mercurius. He was enrolled in the Martenses regiment and feared God.
He was very handsome in appearance, and the whole army loved him because of his skill
and his character. He was originally from the region of Cappadocia by birth. He had been a Christian since childhood, together with his parents.
He was brave in battle, and God was with him in everything he did.
When the tribune saw that he was advancing in his rank and in his military ability, he appointed him chief officer over his regiment.
When the emperor saw the young man’s courage, he loved him and kept him close to him, consulting him about the affairs of the palace.
After these things, while the persecution was spreading, the barbarian nation rose up against the Romans.
The emperor Decius and the entire senate were at a loss because of the great difficulty and helplessness that had suddenly arisen.
The barbarians fought against them so as to take Greater Armenia from them, which lay within their borders, between them and the Romans.
The emperor Decius ordered the military units and all the Roman regiments to assemble, so that they could go out to war and fight the barbarians.
Then the emperor organized the military units and the regiments and marched out to war against the barbarians.
He crossed the Euphrates, the great river that lies within the borders of Armenia. He established his camp in sight of the barbarians and remained near the kings with his army.
It was at that time that the courage of this noble man, Saint Mercurius, the truly faithful man and chief officer of the Martenses regiment, became evident.
For he was a man perfect in his worship of God, conducting his life with complete devotion.
The word of God was always sweeter in his mouth than honey.
One night, as he lay among the army after finishing his prayers, he dozed off for a little while.

And look, an angel of the Lord stood over him, prodded his side, and woke him, with a sword in his right hand. His appearance was terrifying, and he wore a magnificent robe. When Saint Mercurius saw him, he was very afraid.
The angel spoke to him and said, “Mercurius!” He replied, “Here I am, lord.”
Mercurius opened his eyes, and when he saw the angel, he was afraid, thinking that he was one of the emperor’s officials or a military commander.
But he extended toward him the sword he held drawn in his hand, saying to him, “Take this drawn sword from my hand, for with it you will strike down the entire force of the barbarians.
For I am the commander-in-chief of the Lord’s army.
I have come to help you and your fellow soldiers who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Now, then, be victorious and be strong, for I am with you until you complete your struggle in peace.
Look, the time has come, and the contest lies before you.
Fight so that you may receive your strength. An athlete does not receive a crown unless he competes well, and the farmer who labors is the first to receive a share of the crops.
Now, then, listen to the words I am telling you, and do not delay in turning to the Lord your God. For a great struggle awaits you, and you will become a courageous martyr.

For your martyrdom will become known throughout the whole world, and everyone who hears of it will marvel at your courage. They will glorify God for the mighty deeds, the wonders, and the acts of courage that the Lord your God has accomplished for you.
Great tortures and great afflictions await you at the hands of the lawless emperor. But endure, and you will receive the imperishable crown.
And everyone who is worthy to touch your body—I will save him [?].

Even if they are in any kind of distress, or in a court of law, or in a deserted place, or in danger at sea, or on the river, or in extremely severe turmoil, if someone remembers your name in faith and calls upon you, he will be saved.

Whoever builds a shrine in your name and gives an offering in your name on the day of your commemoration, I will place my blessing and lasting prosperity upon their dwelling, and I will never let them lack anything.
Whoever writes the book of your martyrdom, I will tear up the written record of his sins. And I will never remember any of the things he has done, and I will grant him to you as a son in my kingdom.
Look, I have granted you three crowns: one for wealth, one for the sufferings you will endure for my name, and another for your virginity.
Be victorious and be strong, for I am with you.”
After the archangel Michael had said these things to him, he went up to heaven in glory.
When those around him saw the great vision that had appeared, they became like dead men.
The next day, Emperor Decius ordered his army to arrange its divisions and regiments, once they had put on their battle armor and taken their stand for battle against the barbarians.
Then the truly courageous Saint Mercurius charged toward the multitude of barbarians and went into their midst through the power of God, who was with him.
He raised his eyes to heaven and saw the archangel Michael in the appearance of an army commander,

with a drawn sword in his right hand. He held it out toward him and said to him, “Take courage, and take hold of this sword. Charge into the barbarians and slaughter them in the name of Christ, who gives you strength.”
Saint Mercurius stretched out his hand and took the sword from the angel Michael. He charged against the multitudes of barbarians.
He slaughtered them without mercy in the name of Christ, until his hand stuck to the sword because of all the blood, as he struck the barbarians, causing very great and intense suffering that day.
The rest fled and escaped with their lives, as though a fire from heaven had consumed them.

When the emperor saw the courageous deed that Saint Mercurius had performed through the power of God, who was with him, he rejoiced greatly over the victory and this triumph that had come to the Romans.
The emperor bestowed great honors and abundant wealth on Saint Mercurius. He [?] and made him commander of the Martysion regiment.

After these things, Emperor Decius gave orders to all the armies, the divisions, the regiments, and the commanders, as well as the generals, the patricians, and the entire Roman senate, that they should all assemble at the temple of Apollo and offer sacrifices.

Then, when the blessed Mercurius saw the great delusion that had taken hold of the emperor and his army through the devil, he withdrew from them and went into his house. He pleaded with the Lord, saying, “Lord Almighty, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on your creation, which you yourself made, and dispel the stumbling block that the devil has cast into the heart of all humanity.
Give steadfastness to the heart of the people and to everyone who fears your holy name.
Lord, strengthen your churches so that everyone may believe in your holy name. Glory to you, and to your good Father, and to the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.”
When the emperor came to the entrance of the temple, his entire army assembled so that they could all offer sacrifices, each according to his rank.
Saint Mercurius’s turn to offer sacrifice also came, but they did not find him among the army.
When the emperor looked for him, he found him sitting in his house in sackcloth and ashes. grieving deeply over the great division that the devil had brought upon the whole inhabited world.

Then some men from his military unit approached the emperor and accused the blessed Mercurius, saying, “Our lord the emperor, live forever! Your honored authority has ordered people of every nation to sacrifice to the honored gods.

Yet now, look: those who are close to you and attached to you are despising your honored decree. Now Mercurius, who exercises authority in your empire—you exalted him and granted him the rank of count over the military unit,
so that the entire Roman army would obey him, honor him, and submit to him because of the great honor you yourself gave him.

Look, he is despising your authority! He did not assemble with us at the temple to offer sacrifices to the gods. Instead, he went home and stripped himself of his rank. He has disgraced the glory of the Romans and defiled the sacred laws.
We found him inside his house, sitting in sackcloth and ashes, praying in tears to the Lord his God.

He is also persuading everyone to turn away from the worship of the gods. He has made them follow Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified, saying [?], ‘This is God; he himself created heaven and earth.’ In this way he has made everyone withdraw from the gods.”

The emperor said to those reporting these things, “Is what you are telling me about Mercurius, who is attached to me, true— that he despises my gods? But let two of the officials here go and summon him, so that I may find out whether what you are telling me about him is true or not.”
Then the blessed Mercurius was brought before Emperor Decius.
His eyes were full of tears, and he was wearing humble clothing. They made him stand before the emperor.
When the emperor saw him in this humble appearance, he shook his head, bewildered at what had happened.
Then he spoke to him, saying, “Mercurius, tell me what has happened to you, and why you have despised such great honor and the rank
that I gave you. I made you worthy to care for the gods, and you have considered the rank I gave you above all the rest of the army to be nothing.
Now then, tell me where this delusion that has come over you came from.
The Roman army assembled in the temple to offer the gods their due sacrifices, but you alone separated yourself from the military unit.
But tell me who you are, what country you come from, and whether your parents gave you this name.”
The blessed Mercurius answered the emperor, “Do you want to know who I am and what religion I belong to? Listen to my ancestry: in this world I am from Cappadocia.

But in truth I am from the heavenly Jerusalem, the capital city of the saints. And the name my parents originally gave me is Philopator, which means ‘one who loves his father.’ But when I became a soldier, I was named Mercurius by the chief officer of the military unit.
I am a servant of Jesus Christ my Lord, the Son of the living God.
When the king heard these things, he cried out in great anger.
He shook his head and said, “Mercurius, abandon this defiance and madness. Go into the temple and sacrifice to the great god Apollo.
Return to your regiment, to your fellow soldiers, and receive your former rank.”

Saint Mercurius said before the lawless king, “Let this be clear to you, lawless king: I will not sacrifice to your worthless Apollo and abandon my God. He is the one who created heaven and earth and everything.
For I am a Christian.
And I openly renounce military service in this world. I have no need of your rank. I am the servant of Christ Jesus, the Son of the living God.”

King Decius answered him, “Mercurius, until now I have not believed what your accusers told me about you. For I know that they accused you out of envy when they saw the great honor I had given you among the entire regiment and the army.
So now obey me and sacrifice to the gods.
Do not let this matter force me to forget the affection I had for you, take your rank away from you, and inflict severe punishments on you.”
The blessed man answered the king, “Friendship with this world is worthless; it is hostility toward God.
And honors of this kind are temporary.
But the glory of God lasts forever. So now do not trouble yourself in vain. For I am a Christian. I will not sacrifice to your abominable gods. So do whatever you want to me.”

Decius said to him, “Mercurius, sacrifice! Do not die a terrible death.” The blessed Mercurius said to him, “Let one word satisfy you, king: I will certainly not obey you, serve foreign gods, and abandon my God Jesus Christ.”

When Decius heard these things, he became extremely angry. He ordered that Mercurius be stripped of his clothes and stretched out by ten soldiers, and that they beat him with whips of raw ox sinew until the ground beneath him [?] with his blood.
King Decius said to him, “Mercurius, you have tasted the beginning of the tortures and how severe they are. Will you sacrifice or not?”
The blessed Mercurius answered, “As long as I have my Lord Jesus Christ helping him, I do not suffer from your tortures.
For I am the servant of my Lord Jesus Christ, who helps me. He is the king of those in heaven and those on earth.”
When King Decius heard these things, he said, “Mercurius, obey me and sacrifice to the gods. Spare yourself severe tortures, so that you do not die miserably.
Until now I have spared you and been patient with you.”
For I do not want to harm you, especially since you became my companion by fighting for me in the war.
Listen to me and sacrifice to the gods.
Do not ruin your youth with fiery tortures.
I have compassion for your youth and your friendship.

The blessed Mercurius answered, “Every suffering that comes upon me because I confess God will be worth more to me than a holy reward. For the sufferings of the present are not worthy of the glory that will be revealed to us.”

When Emperor Decius heard these things, he said, “If you have set your heart on foolish words, and the honor of the Romans— you have counted it as nothing, and have refused to sacrifice to righteous gods according to the decrees of the senate, and have not obeyed the laws of the emperors, then I, for my part, will punish you as your foolishness deserves, and I will see whether the God in whom you have trusted can rescue you from my hands.”
Saint Mercurius answered and said to the emperor, “It is written in the holy Apostle: ‘Who can separate us from the love of God?
Is it affliction, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are being killed all day long.
For we are convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor authorities, nor things present, nor things to come will be able to separate us from the love of Christ.’”
When the blessed Mercurius said these things, Emperor Decius became angry. He ordered them to put him on the rack and scrape him.
The executioners kept scraping him until the bone of his back was exposed.

But the blessed man did not stop blessing God, saying, “Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of the Father, born of the holy Virgin Mary, who took flesh from the true ewe so that he might redeem the whole race of Adam and free us from slavery to sin, I thank you because you have made us worthy of your great goodness.
Hear me today,
I, your servant Mercurius,
and make me worthy of your holy calling, a sharer in your holy sufferings, and a faithful witness to your divinity.
Now, therefore, my Lord, do not abandon me, and do not be far from me, for afflictions trouble me, and snares have fallen upon me.
But give me strength, my Lord, until I finish my struggle in peace. Do not let my enemies rejoice over me, and do not let them say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”
While he was saying these things, a voice came to him, saying, “Take courage, my farmer Mercurius. Endure, my chosen mighty one!

For I am with you, giving you strength, and I will be with you as your protector, helping you in every suffering.” which you will suffer in my name. Do not grow weak or lose heart before the tortures.
I am with you, giving you strength until you complete your struggle with courage.
Immediately the archangel Michael greeted him and marked his whole body with a seal.
Immediately the torture rack split in two, and the bonds with which he was bound came loose. He sprang up and stood, with no injury anywhere on him, glorifying God.

When the emperor saw what had happened, he was filled with anger and said, “Since this man has said, ‘We have a full suit of armor [?],’ I order that he be stretched out with four ropes and suspended, neither in the sky nor on the ground, a cubit high.”
When they had done this to him, the emperor said, “Where are your weapons now, the ones you rely on? By Zeus, the greatest of the gods, they have stretched you out thoroughly!”

The saint looked up to heaven and said, “Lord, help me! I am your servant.” Again the emperor gave orders to tear his body with sharp instruments, whips, and [?], and then to spread burning coals beneath him, so that he would burn little by little. But the fire was extinguished by the righteous man’s blood as it flowed down.
The saint came to himself with great courage during this further torture.
The emperor Decius had him taken down so that he would not die quickly, and they hurriedly threw him into a dark place.
The soldiers carried him away half dead, with only a little breath remaining in him, thinking that he had died.
A little later, at that very hour, an angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “Peace to you, victorious champion!”
When he had received this, he healed the wounds on his body and set him on his feet, healthy. When he rose, he stood glorifying God, who was helping him.
After this, the emperor ordered that he be brought to stand before the judgment seat.
When the emperor [?] him, he said to him, “They took you away from me half dead. How are you walking now? Perhaps there is not even a wound on your body!”
Then he ordered the guards standing there to examine his body.
They said to the emperor, “Yes, Your Majesty, pious emperor, his whole body is healthy. There is no injury anywhere on him, as though no one had touched him at all.”
Decius himself said, “He will certainly say, ‘It was Christ who healed me.’ Did you bring a doctor into the prison to treat him?”
They said, “By your honored majesty, which rules the whole inhabited world, no human healer has healed him.
Rather, we were wondering how he would die while still alive, or how he recovered—we do not know. For the Christians’ magic is a great deception. Yesterday he [?] burial,
but today he is standing there healthy.”
The emperor was filled with anger and said to him, “Tell me truthfully who healed you, apart from magic.”

Saint Mercurius answered, “My Lord Jesus Christ, the physician of souls and bodies.” He is the one who grants me healing, as he himself said. Sorcerers, conjurers, and idol worshipers are strangers to him. And he will bind them with chains that cannot be undone and hand them over to the fire of Gehenna, because they did not acknowledge the God who created them.
He said, “I will wear out your body with severe tortures. Let me see whether the Christ you believe in will heal you.”
Saint Mercurius said, “I believe in my Lord Jesus Christ. Even if you inflict many punishments on me, you will not be able to shake me.
For he said, ‘Do not fear those who will kill your body but have no power to kill your souls.
Rather, fear him, [?] who has the power to destroy your soul and your body in Gehenna.’”

Then the emperor ordered them to bring a glowing piece of iron and place it under his arms, and burning torches under his sides. But when they did this, instead of smoke, a sweet fragrance arose and spread to everyone in that place. Although they tortured him still more, he did not groan or weep. The emperor said to him, “Where is your physician now? Let him come and heal you! For you said that he has the power to raise [?] even the dead.”

But Saint Mercurius said to him, “Do whatever you want, for you have authority over my body. “But God is the master of my soul. Even if you destroy my body, my soul will endure, remaining imperishable.”
Again the emperor ordered them to hang him upside down, bring a large stone, and hang it from his neck, so that he would suffocate and die quickly.
But the power of God and his grace dwelled in the martyr, and he endured this torture for a long time.

When Emperor Decius saw that the martyr was bearing the punishments with fortitude and that no torture had overcome him, he ordered them to remove that stone from his neck, bring a bronze whip with four lashes, and beat him until the ground was soaked with his blood.
But the brave man stood firm under this further torture, like a stone of adamant in his steadfastness.
And he said, “I thank you, my Lord, because you have made me worthy to suffer for your holy name.”

When the emperor saw that his resolve was unchangeable and that he could not persuade him to offer sacrifice, he took counsel, for he was in a hurry to go to Rome. He sentenced him to punishment by the sword, saying, “Mercurius has insulted the gods and despised the sacred decrees of our benevolence. He has treated our authority as nothing. I order that he be taken to the city in Cappadocia and beheaded there, with everyone watching.
For anyone who has received honor from the emperor, if he opposes his command, will be given blows, and in the end he will be handed over to the sword.”
Those appointed to take him away lifted him, put him on a beast of burden, and tied him onto it, because the martyr’s body had fallen apart all over and had become a corpse.
They traveled along the long road, and within a few days they reached the city of Caesarea. Then they lowered him to the ground little by little.

The Lord stood over him and said to him, “Mercurius, come and rest beside me, because you have completed your race.” You have kept the faith. Receive your crown of glory, which has been appointed for you to inherit.

When the Lord appeared to the martyr, he gained strength. He said to those attending him, “Do what you have been ordered to do, quickly.” The Lord calls everyone to repentance, making you worthy of his grace.
For he is rich, and he gives freely and without envy to those who come to him.
When he had received these things, they cut off his head. He completed his good confession of our Savior on the twenty-fifth of November, that is, Hathor.

A great wonder occurred, worthy of remembrance. After the martyr had completed his course, his body became white as snow, giving off a sweet fragrance like choice incense. Because of this sign, many people became Christians.
They laid the holy man in a prominent shrine, where many miracles and healings take place.
Glory to God the Father and his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, for all ages of ages. Amen.
The martyrdom of Saint Mercurius, the commander and holy martyr of Christ, which he completed on the day [?], namely the twenty-fifth of the month of Hathor. In peace. 99.

In the time of Decius and Valerian, when they were emperors in the great city of Rome, they issued a decree by unanimous agreement, requiring everyone everywhere to sacrifice to the gods and pour out offerings to them.

They summoned all the senators and laid before them what they had devised in this unanimous decision. They found them to be of one mind with them and rejoiced greatly, saying, “We thank our immortal gods, who have revealed this unanimous decision.” And at that very hour,
they ordered a decree to be issued, written as follows in an imperial letter, in this form:

“Decius and Valerian, sovereign and pious emperors, together with all the senators of Rome, write to those who live everywhere. We have considered it necessary to inform you of what is pleasing in our sight.

For long ago we discovered that it is the gods of our fathers who uphold our empire and bestow good things on everyone under our rule. We know their acts of kindness and their gifts, as they have said. Indeed, through them we have enjoyed victory over all nations. Not only that, but they have supplied us with abundant crops through the favorable condition of the air. For this reason, we and all the senators have issued this decree by unanimous agreement and with great earnestness, requiring everyone everywhere, free people and slaves, soldiers and civilians, to bring sacrifices to the gods and pour out offerings to them, with prayers and supplications.

But if anyone undertakes to reject the sacred decree that we have commanded by unanimous agreement, our authority commands that such a person be brought into a dark prison and handed over to severe tortures.”
But whoever obeys our command will receive great honor from us.
But if he disobeys us and our decree, he will be handed over to punishment by the sword, or death by impalement, or be given as food to the wild animals and birds.
Christians in particular will be subject to this sentence.
But those who obey our decree will live in happiness.

When the emperor’s command was proclaimed, the whole city of Rome was filled with turmoil and fear. Not only that, but all the other cities were thrown into turmoil. For this same decree had been sent to them. The governors in each city ordered the crowds to carry out quickly what they had been commanded.
At that time, the barbarians began a war against the Romans.
As they made them turn pale, the Romans in turn prepared their army to fight them. Orders were given for the regiments in every district and city to come and join them.
When they came from each city, eagerly prepared, the regiment of those called the Martysion also came. They were stationed in First Armenia, under a tribune whose name was Sardonicus.
Decius went out to war, while Valerian remained in Rome, administering the affairs of the empire.
The war between the barbarians and the Romans intensified, and they stood facing one another.

After they had continued like this for many days, a man named Mercurius, from the regiment of those called the Martysion, saw a tall man of light. He was wearing glorious clothes and held a drawn sword in his right hand. He said to him, “Mercurius, do not be afraid or lose heart.
For I have been sent to help you and make you victorious.
Take this sword from me and go out against the barbarians. When you defeat them, do not forget the Lord your God.”
In his amazement, he thought that the one speaking to him was one of the emperor’s high officials.

When he had taken the sword and was filled with the Holy Spirit, he went into their midst and killed their leader, along with many others. His arm grew weary from striking, and because of the great quantity of blood, his hand became stuck to the sword’s handle.
This was how the barbarians fled and were slaughtered before the Romans.
Then, when Emperor Decius learned of this mighty man’s courage, he summoned him and gave him high rank. He made him a general and commander over his entire army.

Decius was overjoyed, thinking that he had won the war through the providence of the gods. He distributed large sums of money among the soldiers. That day, the regiments were sent back to their own stations.
He himself held celebrations in every city he passed through on his way to Rome.
One night, while the army was asleep, an angel stood over Mercurius in the form of the man he had seen in battle. He nudged his side and woke him.

When he saw him, he became afraid. The angel said to him, “Do you remember the words I spoke to you in battle, Mercurius? Be careful not to forget the Lord your God, for you must struggle well for his name and receive your crown of victory in the kingdom of heaven, which he has prepared for all who love him.” When he had said these things, he immediately withdrew from him.
When the blessed man came to his senses, he remembered the words and marveled at the power of God’s love for humanity. For he had heard about the Christian faith through his parents.

His father was Gordian, who had been chief officer of this same military unit. The young man was approaching twenty-five years of age. For he had often heard his father say, “Blessed is anyone who serves as a soldier under the King of heaven. He will grant him great, incomparable honors and will fight on his behalf against his enemies.
For that King is the one who created everything by his word.

He established heaven like a vault and adorned it with shining stars, and the earth with beautiful flowers, which give off a sweet fragrance, providing comfort and healing for people. He also made the sea for ships to sail upon, and made it a place for fish to grow.

And he is the one who is coming to judge the living and the dead and to repay each one according to his deeds.” When Saint Mercurius recalled in his heart his father’s words and the revelation he had seen, he was overcome with great astonishment. He began to weep and sigh, saying, “Woe to me, a sinner! I am like a fruitless branch that has withered, having no root in the knowledge of God’s glory.”
While he was still speaking, the emperor immediately sent two of those called silentiaries, with some others, to summon him, because he was his adviser.
He declined to go, saying, “My body is weak.” The emperor left him alone that day. The next day, however, Decius again sent for him in the same way.
When he came to him, they consulted together about the matter at hand.
The emperor said to him, “Let us go, Mercurius, to the great temple of Artemis and offer sacrifices to her.”
When the emperor set out, a great crowd followed him.
But the blessed Mercurius turned back and hid in the praetorium.
Someone accused him before the emperor, saying, “Great emperor, mighty, victorious, and pious, chosen by the gods to govern the entire Roman Empire, allow me to speak, and listen to me with kindness.

Mercurius is the man whom your mighty right hand has exalted and whom you have honored. In the Roman Empire, he did not come with us, as you commanded, to sacrifice in the temple of the great Artemis and make an offering to her according to the decree in force.
The emperor answered, “Who is this?” He said, “Mercurius, the man to whom you gave victory and high rank just three days ago, and whom you raised to an office of still greater importance.
“Not only has he disobeyed Your Majesty, but he has also [?] led many who serve the gods into disobedience.
“If you question him, you will learn the full truth of what I have told you.”

Decius said, “Perhaps envy of this man arose in your heart, and you said these things. But I will not believe you unless I establish the truth with certainty and see the matter for myself, face to face.
“For what is seen with the eyes is considered more reliable than what is heard with the ears.
“So be silent now, and say nothing more against the man. If you have accused him out of envy, as I told you, be assured that you will be liable to severe punishment.
“But if what you have said proves true, you will receive great gifts from us, since you are of one mind with us in your devotion to the gods and the emperors.”

He ordered that Saint Mercurius be brought with the honor previously due to him. When he came before him, the emperor said to him: “Mercurius, was it not I who gave you this great honor and this office, making you commander among all the officials, “because of your wisdom and the victory that the gods granted us in the war? “How, then, have you turned the great affection I have for you into bitter hatred, and reduced these great honors to nothing, “by treating the gods with such utter contempt, as we have been informed out of piety?” Then the truly noble soldier of Christ stripped off the old self with its deeds, according to the words of Paul the apostle, and put on the new self, which had been created within him according to God through baptism. The saint answered in a cheerful and courageous voice, “Keep this sort of honor for yourself. “For although I went out to war and fought, it was not I who won, but the Lord, who granted me the Lord [?].
“Nevertheless, take your honors back, as you have said. For I came naked from my mother’s womb, and naked I will go again.”
After saying this, he stripped off his military cloak, unfastened his belt, and threw them down at the emperor’s feet. He cried out, “I am a Christian! Hear, all of you: I am a Christian!”
Then Decius became like someone beside himself. He gazed into his face for a long time, marveling at his appearance and the beauty of his youth.
The blessed man was very handsome in appearance, radiant in his complexion, with reddish hair, adorned with every kind of beauty
and strength. Many watched him in amazement.
After this, the emperor Decius shook his head and ordered him thrown into prison, saying, “Let the man who did not appreciate honor now experience disgrace.”
He said this because he thought he could change his devout resolve. But as Christ’s martyr was being taken to prison, he rejoiced and exulted in the Spirit, giving glory to God.
That night an angel stood over him and said to him, “Mercurius, take courage and do not be afraid of the tyrant’s threats.

Believe in Christ, who is God, and confess that he is Christ, who is God, for he has the power to save you from every affliction.” The martyr, for his part, became still stronger. These were the things the angel said to him when he appeared to him.

The next day Decius sat on the judgment seat and ordered the blessed man to be brought before him. He said to him, “Does this sort of honor that you have received from me really suit you? It is humiliation that you have chosen for yourself alone.”
The blessed man answered, “It suits me all the more,
for I have received a rank that will never perish.” The emperor said to him, “Tell me your ancestry and your city,
for I know you and the rank to which you belong.”
Saint Mercurius said to him, “If you want to know my ancestry and my city, I will tell you about them.
My father according to the flesh was from Scythia. His name was Gordianus, and he served as a soldier in the Martysion regiment.
At that time he became commander of that same regiment.
But my true Father is God, and my city is the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the great King.”

The emperor said to him again, “Was this name, Mercurius, given to you by your parents, or was it the soldiers who gave it to you?” Saint Mercurius said, “My father named me Philopator, which means ‘one who loves his parents.’
But when I became a soldier, I was given the name Mercurius by the tribune.”

The emperor said to him, “Mercurius, what do you say? Will you obey our decree, which we issued to everyone, worship the gods, and receive your honor as before, along with additional glory? Or, if not, what do you say? Tell us quickly, since you know that you were brought here because of this matter.”
The martyr answered, “As for me, I came here to defeat you and your father Satan, through whom every evil has come about.
When I am victorious, I will be crowned by the true judge of the contest, my Lord Jesus Christ. So do whatever you want quickly, without delay.
For I have the full armor of God and the shield of faith. Through these I will overcome your schemes and all your deceitful tricks against me.”

Then the emperor was filled with rage and said, “Since this man says, ‘I have a full suit of armor [?],’ even though he stands here naked, I order him to be stretched out with four straps and suspended between heaven and earth, a cubit above the ground.”
When they had done this to him, the emperor said, “Where are your weapons now, the ones you rely on? By the great god Zeus, they have stretched you out thoroughly!”
The saint looked up to heaven and said, “My Lord, help me, your servant.”

Again the emperor ordered them to scourge his body with sharp thorns instead of whips. Afterward they spread burning coals beneath him so that he would burn. Little by little, the flame of the fire was extinguished by the righteous man's blood dripping down.
But the saint endured this terrible torture with great fortitude.

Decius ordered them to untie him so that he would not die quickly, and to put him in a dark place and lock him in without delay. The soldiers, the soldiers, lifted him up, half dead, with only a little breath left in him, thinking that he would die.
The soldiers lifted him up, half dead, with only a little breath left in him, thinking that he would die.
A little later, at that very hour, the angel of the Lord appeared to him and said to him, “Peace to you, victorious champion!”
When he had said this, he healed the wounds on his body and set him on his feet, healthy, so that he could rise, stand, and glorify God, who had helped him.
After this, he ordered them to bring him before the judgment seat. When the emperor saw him, he said to him, “They carried you away from me half dead.
How is it that you are walking now? Perhaps there is not even a scar on your body!” Then he ordered the executioners standing there to examine his body.
They said to the emperor, “By your power, pious emperor, his whole body is healthy, without any injury on it, like someone whom they have never even touched with a finger.”
Decius himself said, “Of course he will say, ‘It was Christ who saved me and healed me.’
Did you bring a physician into the prison to treat him?”
They said, “By your honored majesty, which rules over the whole inhabited world, no one treated him.
On the contrary, we thought he was going to die. We do not know how he is alive now or how he recovered.”
He said to them, “You know how powerful the Christians' magic is.
And how is it that yesterday he was a corpse, but today he stands there healthy?”
Filled with anger, he said to him, “Tell me truthfully: who healed you, apart from magic?”
Saint Mercurius answered, “My Lord Jesus Christ, the true physician of our souls and bodies—he is the one who chooses to grant me healing, just as I said.

Sorcerers, conjurers, and idol worshipers are strangers to him, and he will bind them with bonds that cannot be undone and hand them over to the fire of Gehenna, because they did not acknowledge the true God who created them.”
The emperor said, “Then I will destroy your body with severe tortures.
Let me see whether the Christ you trust in will heal you.”
The saint said, “I believe in my Lord Jesus Christ: even if you inflict many punishments on me, you will not be able to shake me.
For he said, ‘Do not fear those who will kill your body but have no power to kill your souls.
Instead, fear all the more the one who has power to destroy your souls and your body in fiery Gehenna.’”
Then the emperor ordered them to bring a piece of red-hot iron and put it beneath his private parts.
And after that, flaming torches beneath his ribs.
When they did this, instead of smoke, a strong, sweet fragrance spread to everyone in that place.
Although they tortured him still more, he neither groaned nor wept.
Decius said to him, “Where is your physician now? Let him come and heal you!
For you said, ‘He has the power to raise me if I die.’”
But Saint Mercurius said to him, “Do whatever you want.
You have authority over my body, but God is the master of my soul.
Even if you destroy my body, my soul will endure, indestructible.”
Again the emperor ordered them to hang him upside down and suspend a large stone from his neck, so that he would quickly die from strangulation.
But God’s power and grace dwelt in the martyr, and he endured this torture for a long time.

When Decius saw that the martyr was enduring the punishments steadfastly, and that no torture had harmed him, he ordered them to remove that stone from his neck, bring a bronze whip with four thongs, and beat him until the ground was soaked with his blood.
But the noble man was like a stone of adamant. He stood firm under this torture. And he said, “I thank you, my Lord, because you have made me worthy to suffer for your holy name.”

When the emperor saw that his resolve was unshakable and that he would not be able to persuade him to offer sacrifice, he took counsel, for he was in a hurry to go to Rome. He sentenced him to death by the sword, saying: “This Mercurius has insulted the gods and scorned the sacred decree of the pagan religion, treating it as nothing. Our sovereign authority commands that he be beheaded in the province of Cappadocia, there in that place, with everyone watching him.

For anyone who has received honors from the emperor, if he opposes his command, will be flogged and finally handed over to the sword.” Those appointed to take him away lifted him up and put him on a pack animal, tying him securely onto it, because the martyr’s body had fallen apart all over and had become like a corpse.
They traveled a long road, and after a few days they reached the city of Caesarea. Then they gently lowered him down.
The Lord stood over him and said to him, “Mercurius, come and rest beside me, for you have finished your race and kept the faith.
Receive your crown of endurance, which has been appointed for you to inherit.”

When the Lord appeared to the martyr, he gained strength. He said to those beside him, “Carry out the orders given to you without delay. May the Lord, who calls everyone to repentance, make you worthy of his grace.
For he is rich and freely bestows gifts, without envy, on those who come to him.”
When he had said this, they cut off his head, and he completed his good confession of our Savior on the twenty-fifth day of the month of November, that is, Hathor.
Then a great miracle occurred, worthy of remembrance.
After the martyr had reached his end, his body became as white as snow, giving off a sweet fragrance like choice flowers and resin.
Because of this sign, many people became Christians.
They laid the saint in a conspicuous place, where many miracles and healings occur,
to the glory of God the Father and his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.
The miracle revealed through Saint Mercurius: how he struck Julian, the lawless emperor, in his camp. This miracle was recorded in the ninth book of the History of the Church. Amen.
At that time, when Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem, a great sign of Christ appeared.
From the third hour of the day until the ninth hour, a great cross of light appeared, standing above the Savior’s tomb in the sight of everyone, believers and unbelievers, barbarians and Romans.
The crowds [?] living in the cities gathered with their food, drink, and wine, and [?] at the cross until it rose into heaven [?] at the ninth hour,
with everyone’s eyes following it.
Cyril, the bishop of Jerusalem, wrote down the miracle that had occurred. He wrote a letter and sent it to Emperor Constantius at the imperial court, who loved Athanasius.
Athanasius presided over the church of Alexandria for another twenty-five years in succession, without any conflict arising against him. For he spent twenty-six years in the episcopate and in exile.
When Constantius died, Julian became emperor in his place.
He was a lawless pagan, born to the sister of Constantine the Great, for her husband was a pagan.
Constantine’s sons saw that the boy was insolent. They feared that he might seize the [?] kingdom from their [?] younger one. They handed him over to the church and made him a reader.
But his father’s people brought him up in paganism. When Constantius died, Julian became emperor in his place.
He immediately devoted himself to paganism and sought to open the temples publicly.
He stayed in the palace at Antioch, for he was not worthy to live in Constantine’s residences.

He went to the place of the pagans and their idols. He took a falcon and gave it to the priest, who offered it as a sacrifice to the demon. The priest took its liver and gave it to him, and he ate it.
Julian was his sister’s son, and he appointed him to the throne.
When he saw the appointed time of his maternal uncle, he seized Saint Theodoric, the priest and steward of the church, and killed him. Then he went and reported to Julian.
But Julian became angry and said, “You have upset me! I do not want to kill them, so that they cannot boast, ‘We became martyrs at your hands.’
Instead, when I return from Persia, I will establish a law for them: Christian commoners must pay three gold solidi per head each year, and a council member three ounces.
By doing these things, he was harassing the Christians in every way.

At that time, the church was rich in the strength of those who bore the Spirit, with four pillars standing beneath it. They were Athanasius of Alexandria, Antony and Pachomius in Upper Egypt, and Basil in Cappadocia.
Basil was Julian’s friend because of the childhood they had spent together at school.
When he heard about Julian’s evil deeds, he came to him with some other servants of God who were his fellow bishops.
When they went in to him, he saw their humble clothing and their belts fastened around them. He said to them, “What are these people looking for?”
Basil answered, “We are looking for a shepherd who is good at tending his flock.”
He said to Basil, “Where did you leave the carpenter’s son when you came here?”
He told him, “I left him making a coffin into which you will be thrown.”
The emperor said to him, “If I were not showing restraint because you are my friend, I would have had your head cut off.”
Basil said to him, “You have not acted wisely. For if you had acted wisely, you would not have abandoned the wisdom you were taught when you were a reader of the books of true wisdom.”
The emperor said to him, “I have read them and understood them.”
Basil said, “You have not read them properly, nor have you ever understood them. For if you had understood them, you would not despise them.”
The emperor said to them, “I will imprison you until I return from Persia, so that you learn what it means to oppose the emperor and have your fill of the misery of imprisonment.”
Basil said, “If you go to Persia, you will not return. Otherwise, God has not spoken through Basil.”
Then Emperor Julian said, “What shall I do to that Galilean, that liar? For he said in his heart, ‘They will not leave one stone upon another in the temple of the Jews.’
But I will rebuild it as an imperial undertaking and prove his words false, so that people will know that he is a liar.”
He ordered Basil to be shut up in prison with the other two who were with him. Then he set out for Persia.

He came to Jerusalem and saw the ruins of the temple, with not a single wall surrounding it, just as Vespasian had destroyed it in the destruction he had carried out. of the Jews. He ordered it to be cleared so that they could rebuild it more splendidly.
Julian appointed a count to oversee the temple, to clear it, lay its foundations, and rebuild it.
He himself set out for Persia and waged war, leaving the saints heaped together for destruction.
Those demolishing the temple cleared it. They did not leave one stone upon another. They did not dismantle it according to the word of our Savior.
They began building. They would build from morning until evening, but when they arrived in the morning, they would find the structures they had built demolished, though not by a human hand.
They spent two months persevering in this way, toiling without any lasting result, since providence was hindering them.
The Jews there told them, “Burn the tombs in which the Christians bury their dead, and you will be able to build.” They listened to them and burned the tombs.
But when they reached the tomb containing John the Baptist and Elisha the prophet, the fire did not touch them.
Although they spent many days with the fire blazing around them, the fire did not touch them.

Some of the brothers gave him money and begged him to allow them to take the bones of the saints. He accepted the money and did as they had asked him. He gave them permission to come at night and take the bones of the saints, John the Baptist and Elisha the prophet.
The hand of the Lord was with them. They wrapped them up to take them to Athanasius in Egypt, because he greatly desired to see them.

They went down to the sea and happened to find a ship. They boarded it, reached Alexandria easily, and gave them to Athanasius. He rejoiced over them when he saw them, as though he had seen them in the flesh.
He hid them in the baptistery while looking for an opportunity to build a shrine for them.
One day he was eating in the garden of our fathers with the brothers. For he would invite the senior clergy every day and eat with them; they would come to him from time to time.
They not only ate but also listened to the words of wisdom that God had given him, as it is written, “Everything for the glory of God.”
Whether it was a time for fasting or a time for eating and drinking, he was always eating and drinking with the word of God.

So he was eating with the brothers, the clergy, and the leading members of the church’s charitable brotherhood in the garden that belonged to him in the district called Hermes, south of the city, overlooking rubbish heaps and open, deserted spaces.
He said, “If I find the opportunity, I will clear away these rubbish heaps and build the shrine of John the Baptist there.”
At that time Theophilus was standing at the table while he ate, because he was his secretary. He heard what Athanasius said and kept it in his heart.
But Julian, following what drove him to go to Persia in anger— Christ Jesus, God, delivered him into the hands of the Persians, because he had left the saints heaped together and gone to Persia.

The death he died happened in this way: at night he saw a multitude of soldiers coming against him out of the air. But then a spear struck him in his kidneys, and he recognized that they were the saints.
Then he took some of his blood and threw it up toward heaven, saying, “Take it for yourself, Jesus! You have taken over the whole place!”
For as soon as he blasphemed, he immediately fell, and God had mercy on his people and saved us. [?] the Romans to their own place.
Now three days before Julian’s death, Basil saw a dream in prison.
When he awoke, he told his two brothers, saying, “Tonight I saw the holy martyr, Saint Mercurius.
He went into his shrine and drew his spear, saying, ‘Am I going to leave this lawless man like this, blaspheming the God of heaven?’
And when he had said this, he went away, and I could no longer see him.”
The other two answered, “Indeed, we too saw this same vision.”

When they saw this decision that God had revealed to them, they believed. They said to one another, “Let us send to the shrine of Saint Mercurius and see whether his spear is set in its place or not.”
So they sent, and they did not find it, and they believed the vision.
Three days later, letters were sent to Antioch saying that the emperor had died in battle.
Then the whole senate, by God’s decree, took Jovian and made him emperor in Julian’s place.
He was a faithful, godly man from his childhood. He immediately released the holy Basil, the pillar of truth, the Cappadocian, together with the brothers.
And so Julian did not return, in accordance with Basil’s words.
In the peace of God. May the prayers and intercessions of the great commander, Saint Mercurius, come down upon us, so that we may all be saved together. Amen.

The martyrdom of Saint Mercurius, the commander, who completed his struggle, which is honored on the twenty-fifth day of this month, Hathor. In the peace of God. May his holy blessings be with us. Amen.
It happened in the twelfth year of Emperor Decius, Valerian and Maximian being Caesar and emperor. He stirred up a persecution against them all and against everyone who professed Christ.
He issued a decree in every city, every region, and every province, requiring every kind of person [?] to sacrifice to the gods [?]. [?] occurred throughout the whole inhabited world at that time.

These are the words written in this decree: “Decius, Valerian, Maxentius, the great sovereign emperor, who rules over the whole inhabited world, [?] writes throughout the inhabited world, and to the regions and provinces under his rule [?]. But we considered it [?] necessary [?] victory [?] the honored gods have revealed themselves to us, in the way they care for us through their good will.” Especially the great victory of this triumph, which is given to us in war, as we are rescued from the hands of our enemies who rise up against us from time to time, so that the ruler of the Romans may receive glory everywhere, while the barbarians submit to us [?]
will punish you.
Immediately he came to drag him off the animal, intending to strike the poor laborer.

Immediately Saint Mercurius moved inside the coffin, and the mule on which he was riding went backward. One of his feet hung down in the saddle. The mule did not stop running with him as he hung behind [?] blind [?].

The mule took on a human voice and cried out, saying, “You misguided people and pagans, whose god has been smashed [?] come out and see the martyr, Saint Mercurius, and Demriam, your son, and believe in Christ, the God of heaven and earth.”
Again the mule ran with him, and did not [?], turning [?].
Oh, how great was the wonder and the spectacle that took place that day!
Not a single person in the whole city stayed behind, whether [?] or great, without coming to the holy martyr, as though they were being driven by a power.
The man himself, his wife, and his children were running after the mule. They were distressed
along with him.
She took the golden idol she worshiped, which was in pieces, and came out into the middle of the city, while everyone watched her with her idol.
Her daughter guided her, as blind people are guided, while she cried out, “Saint Mercurius, look at my humiliation, my great shame, and the shame of my idol, and have mercy on me!”

When she came out, her daughter told her, “[?] the saint [?] in the coffin.” She cried out, “Martyr who received the crown from Christ the King, forgive me, so that I may believe in you and your God, whose name it is not right to utter with an unclean mouth.”
Immediately a white fluid poured down from her eyes as she wept. She could see at once, and her sight was restored as before.
Afterward she took the pieces of the idol and smashed them against one another. She cried out, “Apollo has been put to shame! Christ and his martyr have been honored!”

When her parents saw the healing that had taken place for their daughter, they cried out, “We are Christians! [?] is the God of heaven and his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius. Glory to him forever and ever. Amen.”
The Third Miracle of Saint Mercurius
After this, the Christian people spoke to one another, saying, “Let us bring the martyr’s body into the city.” Others answered, “Perhaps the righteous man does not agree.”
After this they began arguing with one another. Immediately the righteous man moved by himself and went into the city.
The mule cried out, “Sing praise to the martyr!”

And the father of the little boy who was hanging from the beam of the mill cried out, saying, “I beg you, my lord the martyr, just as you gave sight to my daughter, let your mercy also reach my other child, for he has suffered while hanging up there.”
Immediately the martyr set him down on the ground, and he got up and stood, with no injury to his body, not even a bruise, nor did he feel anything at all.
The clergy and the charitable workers sang psalms before him, with lamps burning, choice incense, and fragrant branches, until they brought him into the city.
The man wanted to bring him into his house, but the righteous one would not consent, because his body became as heavy as lead. They could not move him at all.

The crowd cried out, “He will not consent! Let us take him to the church instead.” And he yielded to them, and they took him to the church. They left him there until they built a martyr’s shrine for him, as he deserved [?]. Glory to him forever and ever. Amen.
The Fourth Miracle of Saint Mercurius

Seven days later, all the people of the city were eating and drinking, celebrating with great joy because the saint’s body had been revealed. The father of the little girl to whom the saint had given sight went to the bishop and asked for holy baptism.
He prescribed days of fasting for him. Afterward he baptized him and his entire household in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
They counted the members of his family who had received the light of baptism with him, and found that fifty-three people had been baptized.
After all these things, [?] Saint Mercurius appeared to the poor man as before. He said to him, “Why are you sleeping and remaining idle? Get up and carry bricks to my shrine.”
The man said to him, “My lord, I am poor. I have neither workers nor animals, nor money for expenses.”
The saint said to him, “I will give you everything you need. Only remain a poor man devoted to my house, and do not be of two minds, and you will see my mighty deeds.
When you get up early, go east, to the first street of the city. You will find the little boy whom the mill injured because he wanted to strike you on account of my body.
Say to him, ‘Give me what you have with you, because I need it.’
And he will give you three gold coins, willingly giving them as charity.
I will not let you lack anything. They will bring you so much that you will not know what to do with it.
If he asks you, ‘How did you know that I had anything with me?’ tell him, ‘Mercurius, the one who healed you—
he is the one who told me to tell you.’
And let him also say to his father, ‘You know that when you appealed to me, I quickly listened to you and gave sight to your daughter. I also graciously restored your son to you safe and sound.
If there is still any [?], do some good for your friend the martyr. For if the honor one friend gives another increases until morning, anything beyond this is a burden in every way.’
If he gives you work, do it. If he will not listen to you, feed yourself with these three gold coins until I come to you, God willing. And I will come to you without delay.”
But when he had told him these things, he left him in peace.

Early, when morning came, the man got up and walked along the first street. He came upon the young boy and received the three gold coins. He told him everything that Saint Mercurius had said to him in the vision. The young boy went and told his father these things in fear.
When his father heard these things, he gave glory to God and his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius.

He did not neglect the matter at all, but harnessed his camels, with many hired workers and a large amount of money. He gathered a large quantity of materials and handed them over to the poor man so that he could make bricks.
He also gave him the plow to cultivate the land, and everything else he needed.
One day, while the animals were plowing, one suddenly struck another ox and pierced it with its horns.

When the poor man saw what had happened, he was deeply distressed. He said, “Woe to me because of this! The official [?] has killed his animal. “If only I had not told this young boy about this vision, so that he would tell his father and his father would provide me with a livelihood through this work, only for this great loss to befall me!”

While he was saying these things, Saint Mercurius took the appearance of a city official. He came passing by and saw the man. He walked toward him and acted surprised. He said to him, “Man, why did you leave the animals together until one injured another?
“Its owner will make you pay for it.”
The laborer was deeply distressed, and he was giving glory to the God of Saint Mercurius.
The people who owned the animal heard about it and came to see what had happened. They too were deeply distressed, because it was valuable for its fine appearance and its strength.
Saint Mercurius was sitting at a distance, and no one saw him except the poor man.
They gathered many people around the animal and brought it into the city, to a place by itself. They gave it food to eat, but it would not taste any food at all.
Its owner was deeply distressed over it, because it was strong and had a fine body.
When the people went home, the poor man stayed behind alone with the animal, deeply distressed and thinking about his poverty.
Suddenly Saint Mercurius came in, smiling with a holy smile. He stood beside the poor man’s animal, for he would appear to him face to face.
Smiling, he said to him, “You have wasted no time in [?], brother!”
The man said to him, “Come and see what has happened.”
After this, Saint Mercurius nudged the ox with his foot and said to it, “In the name of Jesus Christ my Lord, get up and do your work without illness.”
It sprang up with great strength, as though it had never been injured at all, and ate some of the fodder.

Immediately Saint Mercurius rebuked the aggressive ox, saying to it, “Your horns will fall off, along with your head.” You will never again be able to say it to any human being or animal, but you will be tame forever.
Immediately his horns came loose, fell off, and separated from his head, and he became tame.
The poor man bowed down before Saint Mercurius and said to him, “A little favor, my lord, martyr of Christ Jesus, for whose holy name you bore witness.”
Immediately Saint Mercurius hid himself from him.
The man went out rejoicing and shouting, saying, “Saint Mercurius appeared to me! He healed the calf and rebuked the unruly calf, and it became sensible.”
A crowd came to see what had happened, and they all shouted, “The God of Saint Mercurius is one! Glory to him forever and ever! Amen.”
The fifth miracle of Saint Mercurius
After these things, they began working at making bricks for the shrine of Saint Mercurius. A pagan official also came near the workers who were making bricks for the shrine of Saint Merius.

He quickly set up his own brickmaking site beside them, since he too wanted to build a courtyard at his house. One day he came and sat beside the workers who were working. He got up and inspected the bricks until he reached the saint’s bricks, and he desired the saint’s bricks more than all his own.
He said, “Indeed, I will take a hundred loads of bricks from these Christians’ bricks and tell the workers that they made them for me.
And if they say, ‘We will not let you take them,’ I will beat them and take them against their will. Then I will see what this fellow called Mercurius will do to me.”
He went home that day.

A few days later, he went and looked at the saint’s bricks, and he sighed deeply, because the people of the city, small and great, were each sending a worker every day to work, since they wanted to build a martyr’s shrine for him.
Then the pagan man became intensely jealous of the saint’s bricks, with a great jealousy inspired by the devil.
After this, he summoned the poor man to whom Saint Mercurius had appeared. He said to him, “Come and show me the boundary between my bricks and yours, because I want to build my house.”
The man said to him, “Your men know the number of your bricks.”
He said, “I have brought no one with me except you. But as far as I remember, these are mine up to this point.”

The man was astonished and said to him, “Man, do not harm your soul! Do not touch this saint’s bricks, or punishment will overtake you. But if you take them, I will find out your strength and your might.” And the pagan gave the poor man a [?].

He said to him, “Since you said, ‘That fellow will strike you,’ I will take more than these, so that I can find out how strong you and that fellow are.” “What will he do to me?” The man said to him, “Do as you please. Look, the God of Saint Mercurius sees you, but you will not overcome him.”
The man immediately sent one of his slaves, with great arrogance. The slave went and brought camels, and the man walked ahead of them with great arrogance.

He began loading the camels with the saint’s bricks. He stood in front of a large male camel that belonged to him and ordered his slaves, with great arrogance, to load the camels with bricks. He said, “Let me now see the power of this Mercurius!”
Immediately, before the words had left his mouth, the camel in front of which he was standing opened its mouth, seized the pagan official, threw him down beside itself, and lay on top of him.
And immediately, behold, Saint Mercurius came riding his spiritual horse and stood beside the camel that had seized the man. He struck him with his spear on his left foot, and [?]
“Now he is threatening me, saying, ‘Are you the one who will plunder my shrine, hanging by just one foot?’”
The crowd followed him in fear and trembling until he reached the foundation of the sanctuary, hanging upside down.
The man cried out, saying, “My lord, Saint Mercurius, forgive me for my ignorance! And all my bricks—
I will give them to you for the building of your sanctuary. I will also deliver to you every good piece of timber, along with all the materials I have gathered for my house.
I will become a Christian, together with my whole household. I will set my slaves free, and I will become a caretaker of your sanctuary until the day of my death.”
When he had said these things, the camel put him down on the ground. Saint Mercurius touched his wounds and healed him, and released him without any wound anywhere on his body.
Great fear seized everyone standing there, as they saw how the camel had injured him.
The man declared to them, “I saw Saint Mercurius stabbing me with a spear.” Then the man’s body was examined, but they found no wound anywhere on it.
They asked him, “Where is the wound on your body? Especially since you were crying out, ‘Look, the righteous one is stabbing my foot with his spear!’”
The man said to them, “From the moment the camel released me and he touched my whole body, I was healed.”
Immediately the man went to the bishop, who baptized him and his entire household. He also set all his slaves free.
He gave all the materials he had gathered for building his house, along with the timber, the stones, and all his bricks.
He delivered them to the sanctuary, along with fine gold and a large sum of money.
He worked with his own hands, together with all his men, and all his animals worked without payment.
He would say to the workers, “Go on and build the house of this mighty one!”
He died, as is the fate of everyone, before they finished the shrine.
Glory to God and to his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius!
The sixth of the miracles of Saint Mercurius.
Now when they began building the martyr’s shrine of Saint Mercurius, with great [?], there were abundant materials and many people working at the saint’s sanctuary.
After this, a man from the city came passing by. He saw the building materials at the site of the martyr’s shrine and was amazed. He coveted a piece of wood that was lying there.
He said, “I need this [?] piece of wood, and I will take it.”
He went over to the wood, lifted it onto himself, and walked off with it until he had gone a little way into the city.

Then he became lost and did not know where he was going, because the saint had confused his mind. Eventually he came and stood at the door of the poor man who was the caretaker of Saint Mercurius’s shrine.
This was the man to whom he would appear. He did not know where he was going.

And behold, the saint spoke to the caretaker, saying to him, “What are you doing sitting here? Look, someone has stolen wood from my sanctuary. But get up and go to the door of your house. You will find the man with this piece of wood loaded onto him, wandering about without knowing where he is going. For I am the one who confused him. I did not let him know where he was going until he came to this place, so that you would see him with the piece of wood he stole loaded onto him.”
When he saw the house, he opened for him, and he recognized him as the steward of the martyr’s shrine. His senses returned to him.
Immediately he cried out, “There is one God, the God of Saint Mercurius! Have mercy on me! Do not be angry with me or bring harm upon me, for I have sinned against you and stolen your wood.”

Then the saint again said to his caretaker, “Tell the man this: ‘Why do you not come and do a day’s work at my sanctuary? The wood that he gave to my sanctuary as an offering for the salvation of their souls—you went and stole it! But because of God’s compassion, look, I have forgiven you. Take the wood and put it back in its proper place, and go home.’ When he gets up in the morning, let him proclaim what he has done, so that the others will be afraid and will not steal the materials from my sanctuary again, lest I bring harm upon them.”
When he had said these things, he disappeared from his sight.
The poor man got up and came outside. He found the man standing at the door of his house with the wood loaded onto him, not knowing where to go.
He was saying, “Saint Mercurius, have compassion on me and have mercy on me, for I have sinned, my lord!”

The poor man spoke to him: “My dear brother, where are you coming from with the wood loaded onto you? I tell you, this wood belongs to Saint Mercurius. Now tell me everything that has happened to you.”
The man told him how he had taken the wood and how Saint Mercurius had confused his mind until he came to the door of the poor man’s house, unaware of what he was doing.
The man of Saint Mercurius [?] passed on to the man who had taken the wood every word that Saint Mercurius had spoken to him.

When the man heard these things, he was amazed and said, “Not just [?] one single day! Rather, if the God of Saint Mercurius grants me health, I will not stop working at his sanctuary until it is completed. And I will proclaim his power everywhere I go.”
Immediately he came to his senses. He went home, giving glory to God and his holy martyr, and slept until morning.
When daylight came, he proclaimed to the whole city what had happened.

He went to the place from which the timber was being taken out, lifted it onto his neck while everyone watched, and carried it to the saint’s shrine. He put it in the place from which he had taken it.
Great fear fell upon everyone who saw him, and they did not touch any other property belonging to the shrine again until they had completed it.
The man did not stop working, molding bricks for the saint’s shrine, until they had completed it.
And he gave glory to the God of Saint Mercurius.
The Seventh Miracle of Saint Mercurius
Listen again, my beloved, to another great wonder, to the glory of the God of Saint Mercurius.
When they had beautifully constructed the shrine with every kind of craftsmanship, they fitted it with a wooden railing made of jujube wood.
For there were three large pieces of jujube wood belonging to the woman to whom Saint Mercurius had given sight. Her late husband had designated them before he died, and she had them as a large beam.
Then God [?] visited him, according to the fate of every human being. He died and left her a great deal of property.
Then they constructed the arch of jujube wood, making it very beautiful.

When the crowds gathered to raise it, a few of the workers said to one another jokingly, “If only the heart of Saint Mercurius is pleased with us for building him a martyr’s shrine, let him make the arch of jujube wood produce abundant fruit, if he is satisfied, so that we can eat from it.”
Suddenly, while the words were still coming out of their mouths, the wood put out branches laden with fine, ripe jujubes.
When the crowds saw what had happened, they cried out loudly, giving glory to God and his holy martyr, who performs these many miracles and wonders.
Some devout people took some of the fruit and kept it with them in their homes as a protection.
Oh, how many healings took place through those fruits! The crowds ate and were satisfied, and they gave thanks to God and his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius.

Everyone in the city and its surrounding area heard about it, both young and old, and they all came together to see the great wonder. Men and women came to look at what had happened, which the righteous man had brought about.
There was also a Jew in the city called Gaius. He was harsh [?] toward everyone, but especially toward Christians.
He too heard about the great wonder that had taken place in the saint’s shrine. He said, “I will go and see whether these things the Christians are saying are true or not. Perhaps they are lying.”

He gave orders—[?] he was a servant of the serpent—for a white female mule to be saddled for him. He mounted it and said to his servant, “Come, let us see the ridiculous thing the Christians are doing.”
Then they traveled together until they reached the shrine of Saint Mercurius. The Jewish man went inside mounted on his animal.
One of the young Christian children who were carrying clay [?] to the shrine said to him, “Are you going [?], you godless man, with this animal into God’s church?”
The Jewish man paid no attention to him at all. Instead, he went and stood looking up at the tomb, which was laden with fruit and leaves, as though it were growing in the ground.
The Jewish man said, “Who is putting these foreign leaves on the wreaths, falsely claiming that the saint is the one who did this?”

The young son of Aphthartus, who had spoken earlier about the animal he was riding, answered him, saying, “The one who will strike you this very hour— he is the one who reveals all the wonders.” Immediately the man became filled with anger and great fury. He drove the animal at the little boy to strike him.
Immediately the mule’s four feet sank into the ground as though it were mud. He fell on his face and injured himself on the stones and bricks lying about at the building site.
Immediately Saint Mercurius came through the doorway, with an angel walking beside him and his spear in his hand.

He said to him, “What are you doing here, you worthless man? This is no place for mockery. You let your horse come inside. Are these leaves and these fruits foreign? And you have come here to strike those working on my shrine. You have not worked yourself, nor have you left the workers alone.”
Immediately he stabbed him with his spear in the middle of his belly, and his intestines came out. No one could see the saint except the Jewish man whom the saint had struck.
But they could see the man lying there unconscious, and they did not know what had happened to him.

Afterward the man cried out loudly, saying, “Saint Mercurius, help me in this hour of distress! I will never again meddle with anything belonging to the saint. And if you have mercy on me and deliver me from this affliction, I too will become a Christian, and I will erect your memorial image. I [?] you now in your glory, with your spear piercing me. I will also have my own image made, lying at your feet in great shame and helplessness. I will gild your image with refined gold and fiery-colored stones, namely chrysolite. And I will have the image of your spear set with genuine diamond stones. Help me, my lord Mercurius!”
When he had said these things, he lay there half dead.

After this, the angel of the Lord spoke to Saint Mercurius: “Withdraw your spear from him, if he will believe in our true king, Christ. A sinner is better than a righteous person who is going to sin. There is joy among the angels over a sinner when he repents of his sins, just as the Savior taught his disciples. Leave him there. Let mercy reach him, for he is ignorant.”
And the saint released him.
When he came to his senses, he related everything that had happened to him to the crowd gathered there. They glorified God, who performs these miracles through his holy martyr.

After this, the man got up and went to his house, speaking to his wife and his servants. all the things that had happened to him, and that he had no children because his wife was barren. The next day,
he said to his wife, “Let whoever desires God follow me.”
He took his wife and his servants and went to the bishop. The bishop baptized them in the name [?] of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
And he named him Zechariah, and his wife Elizabeth.
When he went home, he had intercourse with his wife, and she conceived two boys at the same time.
When the nine months were completed, she gave birth to twin sons.
She named the firstborn Mercurius, after the saint, because they had received deliverance through him. They named the second John, after the Baptist.
