After all this, he summoned a craftsman and gave him ten pounds of fine gold and precious genuine gemstones. He made an image of Saint Mercurius with his spear in his hand, and he had it inlaid with diamonds.
He also had his own image made of gold and genuine gemstones, beneath Saint Mercurius, who was striking him in the heart with his spear.
He brought his image into the church. After the consecration of the sanctuary, he placed it in front of the chancel, where it remains to this day.
They now stand as a testimony to the miracles of the holy martyr, Saint Mercurius. In the peace of God. Amen.
The Eighth Miracle of Saint Mercurius
Now it happened, after the saint’s sanctuary had been consecrated, that the news of these miracles spread everywhere.
A great crowd came to his holy relics and paid homage before them. The sick received healing and went home.
He cast out demons, and they brought many votive gifts and offerings into his sanctuary.
There was an official in a village near the place [?]. That official’s name was Lord Hermapollon.
He had a little daughter, his only child. He had never had any other children besides her.
He had left her a little orphan, and he watched over her as though he were looking at God.

He heard about the miracles of Saint Mercurius, got up, and took a small gift of thirty gold coins. He went to the saint’s sanctuary, prayed, and gave the thirty gold coins to the sanctuary’s steward.

The clergy gave him an earnest invitation, for those clergy were hospitable people. Then they drank a great deal of wine and ate a great deal of food while entertaining the official. Then a conversation arose among them.
The official said, “What do you need? Tell me, and I will provide it for this sanctuary.”
The clergy and the steward said to him, “We want a good resting place on which to lay the martyr’s body.”

The governor answered, saying, “If the God of Saint Mercurius grants this request, I will prepare a resting place for the martyr and decorate it with precious ivory, like those of the Roman emperors.”

After this, the governor went to sleep that night, and Saint Mercurius appeared to him in the form of a military commander. He said to him, “When you get up, mount your animal and go home. Do not delay in preparing this coffin as you said. For I know that you will be somewhat negligent about the dimensions of the resting place that the clergy told you about this evening. But I do not hold it against you. I know that later you will [?] come to my shrine, and I will have mercy on you.”
The governor awoke from the vision and was greatly amazed.
When morning came, he went to the church and bowed down over the martyr’s body. He went outside, mounted his animals, and went home.

When a day had passed since the governor returned from the saint’s shrine, a governor of the city heard about his unmarried daughter, that she was very beautiful. He sent people from the city to him, saying, “I want to take your daughter as a wife for my son. I will make the bride-price generous, with gold and silver, male slaves and female slaves, camels, and sailors who sail the sea—all in keeping with the honor of your high rank.”
Then the girl’s mother, the governor’s wife, called him and told him about the matter.

The governor said, “Even if [?] a young man whom I had brought into my house and to whom I had assigned all my income, I could never part with her. As for children, I have none besides her. I look to her as I look to God.”
Then the governor’s wife told everything to the women who had come. They went away distressed and told the young man and his parents everything. They were grieved and said nothing.
When evening came, they called their son and spoke with him about many young women in the city. But they did not please the young man; instead, he was distressed,
because he knew that the girl was very beautiful. Since he was little, when he was in school with his teacher,
the teacher would send the boy every day, and he would tell the girl what his teacher had written for him on his tablet.
So he spent the whole night lying down, thinking about what he could do to unite with the girl, whether through marriage or through illicit sex,
because of his great passion for her. In short, he remained distressed and told no one about his distress.
Within a month after these things happened, the young man’s mother died. Because of the grief over his mother, his father did not look for another wife for him.
As for the young man, the thought of the girl never stopped troubling him. He grew worse every day until he was near death.
He also visited many magicians, wanting to influence her parents’ minds so that they would give him the girl [?]. But he did not succeed in this.
At last he found a powerful magician, who said, “I will make you see her and speak with her face to face many times.” But the young man, because of his great desperation for [?]
They also fitted together pieces of pinewood [?] and covered them with sheets of ivory.
They also made the resting place and inlaid it with an image of the martyr in beautiful colored stones, together with three gold crosses and three silver seals.

Finally, they finished it beautifully, with great care. That night he loaded the chest onto his pack animals, along with his wife and his sick daughter, and his servants, until they reached the saint’s shrine two days later, for the feast of Saint Mercurius, which falls on the twenty-eighth of Hathor.
When the clergy saw the chest, they were greatly amazed. They sang psalms before it and brought it into the church.
The governor, his wife, and his daughter entered the martyr’s sanctuary and bowed down over the saint’s body with great joy.
The steward took them to a private place, and they rested [?] from the hardships of the journey.
Their daughter was suffering torment, because that illness hated the church, since it was a demonic affliction. Now, in the middle of the night,
[?] Saint Mercurius dressed himself like a military commander and went to the governor’s city. He entered the house of the young man who had brought the tormenting illness upon the little girl.
He appeared to him in a terrifying way, with his sword drawn in his hand. In anger, he struck him [?] with the sword three times.
He sprang up from sleep and saw the saint standing over him, face to face. He jerked himself up on his bed, intending to get up and flee.
Immediately he fell on his face at the saint’s feet, and the saint continued flogging him for a long time, threatening him.
He kissed the saint’s feet, saying, “Woe to me! I am a sinner!” And he wept, saying, “What sin have I committed, my lord?”
The saint said to him, “Have you not heard what is written: ‘Do not curse the ruler of your people, nor raise your hand against the Lord’s anointed’?”
He said, “It is written, my lord. But tell me your name, and tell me my sin, so that I may repent of my sin. For I know that repentance is possible.”

The saint said to him, “I am Mercurius, who performs miracles in this city, Caesarea. I have come to strike you and your magician, who violently inflicted this great torment on the only daughter of Hermapollon of this city. But since I have found repentance in you, I will not strike you this time. When you get up early, however, do not neglect this. Go to the magician, the man who committed the sin, and come together to my shrine. Then your joy will be complete in every way.”
The man said to him, “I will gladly come myself, but that man certainly will not come.”
Saint Mercurius answered him, “Save yourself, and [?] have that man come in disguise.”
Then the saint vanished from his sight.
When morning came, he went straight to my father and said to him, “My father, help me, for I want to go to the shrine of Saint Mercurius and pray.”

His father was very fond of him, because he had no one besides him. He said, “Go, my son, but do not be slow to return and leave my heart longing for you, O light of my eyes.” He also gave him a large sum for expenses and three male servants to travel with him.
Then he hurried along the road in great haste, heading for the city where the magician lived.
He said to him, “Get up! Let us go to the shrine of Saint Mercurius and pray.” And he told the magician everything that had happened to him.

When the magician heard that the man and his daughter were at the saint’s martyr shrine [?], he became afraid. The magician said, “Even if I am summoned now, I will not come to the shrine of Saint Mercurius, lest he expose me and the little girl’s father kill me because of his daughter.”

Immediately the young man hurried with great energy until he reached the saint’s martyr shrine. In great fear, he bowed down over the saint’s body. He saw the little girl lying prostrate over the saint’s body, with her father and mother pleading with him and seeking help for her.
The saint was leaving her in good health. The young man called the steward and gave him ten gold coins.

The official, who was the little girl’s father, looked [?] and saw the young man. He recognized him and went over to him. He knew nothing about the matter. He greeted him and asked him about the well-being of his household.
After the two of them had prayed, he invited the young man and took him upstairs to the place where he was staying. They ate and drank together. He saw the little girl and was very happy.

Yet he was distressed about her because she was suffering, and he felt ashamed before her parents because [?] of her illness. He was also afraid that the martyr would expose him. In short, there were many worries in the young man’s heart.

Saint Mercurius appeared to the little girl’s father. He woke him from sleep and took him outside the place where he was sleeping. He told him, “Give your daughter to the young man who is with you, if you want me to heal her for you. And do not seek to harm him, lest you cause her to suffer [?] even more than this.”

He also told him, “There are three more [?] before his father passes away, for his lifetime has come to an end. And do not neglect to give him your daughter after his father’s death.” He also told him how the young man had used magic on his daughter, causing her to become ill because of his desire for her. He also told him how he himself had appeared to the young man and threatened him to stop him, and about everything that had happened to the young man until he came to the martyr shrine.
When Saint Mercurius had said these things, he vanished from his sight. The official awoke from the vision and smelled a strong, exquisite fragrance.
He said, “Truly, it was Saint Mercurius who came and appeared to me.”

He remained there, reflecting on what the young man had done to his daughter because of his desire for her. He kept wondering to himself, “Does the saint want me to reveal the secret, or should I keep it hidden?”

While he was thinking about these things, a trumpet was sounded so that everyone who was sleeping would rise, come to the church, and sing hymns with the devout workers [?], for it was the saint’s great feast, which falls on the twenty-eighth of Hathor. The crowds rose and came joyfully to the church dressed in white.
They continued singing hymns until daylight spread.

The man also rose and called his wife and daughter, and they came to the shrine, with their servants following them. The young man also came with his servants. They went and bowed down over the saint’s body.
While they were rejoicing, the young man searched the sleeping place, wondering about his master. He found the magician tied to the martyr’s [?], like a dog keeping silent.
When he saw the young man, he cried out, “Woe to me, my lord and brother! Come and see my great humiliation!”
The young man said to him, “How did you come to be in a place like this?”
The magician said to him, “My brother, after you left me, Saint Mercurius came to me. He put a muzzle on me, brought me here, and tied me up in this sleeping place, to my shame.”
Immediately he cried out, “Help me, my beloved brother! While I am speaking with you, the saint has struck me in the face, and I have been utterly disgraced!”
He said to him, “A mystery that you were not told about in order to reveal it—why are you seeking to reveal it?”

And immediately a demon sprang upon the magician, untied him, and threw him onto the ground, crying out, “Let me punish him! Saint Mercurius is the one giving me orders, because the blasphemies he has uttered against the God who created him are great.”
There was also a woman whom a demon had thrown down beside the saint’s body.
When the congregation was dismissed, the whole crowd gathered to watch how the saint humiliated the demons.
And the governor himself also came and sat down.

The demon-possessed woman cried out, “Hermapollon, [?] the evil of this magician, for he has bewitched your daughter. And give your daughter to the young man, just as you were told in the vision, lest Jesus reject your [?] for healing. Do not neglect to betroth your daughter to the young man, for the young man’s father has only another three months. After this, your heart will be at ease.”
His wife was bewildered by what she was hearing. And immediately, [?], her daughter was freed from her torment, as though she had never been ill at all.

The woman, through whom Saint Mercurius was speaking, said to the magician, “From this moment on, you must not live among people. Instead, you must flee far away and live alone in the desert, practicing self-discipline until the day of your death.”
He rebuked the spirit within him and drove it out. His sight was fully restored, and he went into the desert and lived in seclusion until the day of his death.
When the festival day had passed, Hermapollon mounted his animals with his wife, his daughter, and his servants. The young man also went with his servants, and they returned to their city.
The governor told his wife everything the saint had said to him in the vision.
His wife realized that what the governor had told her about the vision was also what the saint had said through the mouth of the demon-possessed woman.
When the people heard, great agreement arose among them. They sent [?], and [?] with him.
They told him, “Take care of the arrangements, and let us celebrate the wedding, just as Saint Mercurius told us.”
When the young man heard this, he rejoiced greatly. When the meal was over, the young man went home and told his father everything, and his father rejoiced even more.
When morning came, the young man’s father gathered all the wealthy leading men of the city. They came to the house of Lord Hermapollon and spoke with him about his daughter.
And they came to an agreement with one another and gave her a great deal of gold and silver, many ornaments, male and female slaves, and fishermen who sailed the sea.
And they brought public entertainers [?], rope dancers [?], organ players, mime actors, flute players, and comic performers [?]. They celebrated the wedding with great splendor.
And after another week, they invited many rich people and many officials. They celebrated the wedding with great worldly splendor and rejoiced greatly.
And within three months after the wedding, the young man’s father died at a very advanced age.

And when the days of mourning for him were over, the young man took his gold, his silver, and all his possessions, and his slaves, and brought them to his father-in-law’s house. They stayed together until the day of their death.
And every year they came to the shrine of Saint Mercurius on his holy feast day, praying and giving thanks to God for his great mighty deeds.
You have seen, my beloved, these great favors that God grants his chosen ones from time to time. I wish, O God-loving people, to tell you a few things.
But I know that no one can reach the end of the mighty deeds of the saints, especially those of the martyr Saint Mercurius.
And again, moderation is good in everything. Oh, blessed are all who read!
